title: State of Compliance November 2026: Federal and State Compliance Updates
summary: Stay ahead of 2026 HR compliance updates with key changes to tax year 2027 inflation adjustments, retirement plan limits, tip income reporting, Trump Accounts, paid family and medical leave, unemployment insurance, minimum wage and overtime, pay transparency, personnel records, withholding requirements and more.
body_markdown:
Paycom is committed to helping HR professionals navigate the ever-changing compliance landscape. In this edition of State of Compliance, we look at changes across 15 states and at the federal level. Please note that this list is not intended to be comprehensive. Our team is constantly monitoring for updates that may impact your organization.


## Federal HR compliance updates


The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) **corrected the 2026 General Instructions for Forms W-2 and W-3** to clarify that the maximum exclusion for employer-provided dependent care benefits is $7,500, not $5,000 as originally published. The updated limit applies beginning with the 2026 tax year.


Employers must report all dependent care benefits paid or incurred during the year in Box 10 of Form W-2, including amounts above the exclusion limit and amounts employees forfeit.


For more information,[visit the IRS website](https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/correction-to-the-dependent-care-benefits-exclusion-amount-in-the-2026-general-instructions-for-forms-w-2-and-w-3) .


The IRS released **Form 8027, Employer’s Annual Information Return of Tip Income and Allocated Tips** , and its instructions for reporting 2026 tip income and allocated tips. Employers that operate large food or beverage establishments must file the form annually to report receipts and tips, and to determine allocated tips for tipped employees.


An establishment is considered a “large food or beverage establishment” if it is located in the 50 states or the District of Columbia, tipping is customary and the employer normally employed more than 10 employees on a typical business day during the preceding calendar year. Employers must file a separate Form 8027 for each location.


The 2026 form includes a new line B, which asks whether the establishment participated in a voluntary tip-reporting program during the calendar year. Employers must check either the “Yes” or “No” box. Employers must also continue to check “Yes” or “No” on line A to indicate whether the establishment accepts credit cards, debit cards or other charges. If “Yes” is checked, lines 1 and 2 must be completed, including an amount, even if zero.


Employers must allocate tips among directly tipped employees if total tips reported during a payroll period are less than 8% (or the approved lower rate) of the establishment’s gross receipts for that period. Allocated amounts must be shown in Box 8 of Form W-2.


The IRS retired the Filing Information Returns Electronically (FIRE) system. The Information Returns Intake System (IRIS) is now the only system available to electronically file Form 8027. Employers required to file 10 or more information returns during the year must file them electronically.


Form 8027 is due March 1, 2027, or March 31, 2027, if filed electronically. Employers may request an extension of time to file using Form 8809.


For more information, visit the[IRS website](https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/about-form-8027) .


The IRS announced the **tax year 2027 annual inflation adjustments** for almost 70 tax provisions, including tax rate schedules, standard deduction amounts and other payroll-related thresholds. Details are provided in[Revenue Procedure 2026-35](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/rp-26-35.pdf) . The adjustments generally apply to tax returns filed in 2028.


For tax year 2027, the standard deduction increases to $33,200 for married couples filing jointly, up $1,000 from 2026. The standard deduction rises to $16,600 for single taxpayers and married individuals filing separately, and is $24,925 for heads of households.


The top tax rate remains 37% for single taxpayers with incomes greater than $661,375 ($793,650 for married couples filing jointly). The other rates for single taxpayers are:


- 35% for incomes over $264,550 ($529,100 for married couples filing jointly)
- 32% for incomes over $208,325 ($416,650 for married couples filing jointly)
- 24% for incomes over $109,125 ($218,250 for married couples filing jointly)
- 22% for incomes over $52,025 ($104,050 for married couples filing jointly)
- 12% for incomes over $12,800 ($25,600 for married couples filing jointly)
- 10% for incomes of $12,800 or less ($25,600 or less for married couples filing jointly)


Other notable 2027 amounts for employers and payroll teams include:


- **Qualified transportation fringe benefit and qualified parking:** The monthly limit increases to $350, up $10 from 2026.
- **Health flexible spending arrangements:** The limit for voluntary employee salary reductions increases to $3,500, up $100. For cafeteria plans that permit carryover, the maximum carryover amount is $700, up $20.
- **Employer-provided childcare tax credit:** The maximum credit rises to $515,943.67, up from $500,000 in 2026 ($619,132.40 for an eligible small business).
- **Child tax credit:** The maximum amount is $2,300, up $100, and the refundable portion is $1,800, up $100.
- **Adoption credit:** The maximum credit is $18,250 in qualified adoption expenses, up from $17,670, with up to $5,280 refundable.
- **Earned income tax credit:** The maximum amount is $8,496 for taxpayers with three or more qualifying children, up from $8,231.
- **Foreign earned income exclusion:** The exclusion is $137,300, up from $132,900.


For more information,[visit the IRS website](https://www.irs.gov/newsroom/irs-releases-tax-inflation-adjustments-for-tax-year-2027-taxpayers-continue-to-benefit-from-the-working-families-tax-cuts) .


The IRS announced that the **401(k) contribution limit** for 2027 will increase to $25,500, up from $24,500 for 2026. The limit also applies to 403(b) plans, governmental 457 plans and the federal government’s Thrift Savings Plan. The limit on annual contributions to an individual retirement account (IRA) remains $7,500, and the IRA catch-up contribution limit for individuals age 50 and older remains $1,100.


The catch-up contribution limit for employees age 50 and older who participate in most 401(k), 403(b), governmental 457 and Thrift Savings Plans increases to $8,500, up from $8,000 for 2026, so these participants can generally contribute up to $34,000 in 2027. Under SECURE 2.0, employees ages 60 through 63 have a higher catch-up limit of $11,750 for 2027.


Other 2027 limits and income ranges include:


- **Traditional IRA deduction phase-out (covered by a workplace plan):** $83,000 to $93,000 for single taxpayers, up from $81,000 to $91,000 in 2026, and $133,000 to $153,000 for married couples filing jointly, up from $129,000 to $149,000. For an IRA contributor who is not covered by a workplace plan but is married to someone who is, the range is $250,000 to $260,000, up from $242,000 to $252,000.
- **Roth IRA income phase-out:** $158,000 to $173,000 for singles and heads of household, up from $153,000 to $168,000 in 2026, and $250,000 to $260,000 for married couples filing jointly, up from $242,000 to $252,000.
- **Saver’s Credit income limit:** $83,000 for married couples filing jointly, $62,250 for heads of household and $41,500 for singles and married individuals filing separately.
- **SIMPLE retirement accounts:** The contribution limit increases to $17,500, up from $17,000 in 2026. The higher limit for certain applicable SIMPLE plans increases to $19,100, up from $18,100. Catch-up limits remain unchanged.


For more information, see[IRS Notice 2026-66](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/n-26-66.pdf) on the IRS website.


Employers with workers covered by **state paid family and medical leave programs** should prepare for federal withholding and reporting requirements expected to apply in 2027.[IRS Revenue Ruling 2025-4](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/rr-25-04.pdf) explains the federal income and employment tax treatment of contributions and benefits, while[Notice 2026-6](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/n-26-06.pdf) extends transition relief through 2026.


Under the guidance, family-leave benefits generally are included in an employee’s income and reported on Form 1099 but are not treated as wages for federal employment tax purposes. Medical-leave benefits attributable to employer contributions generally are treated as taxable wages and may create federal withholding, employment tax and Form W-2 reporting obligations.


Employers should continue monitoring IRS and state guidance before the transition relief expires.


The IRS has issued revised **December 2026 instructions for Forms 1099-MISC and 1099-NEC** , introducing several reporting updates that affect how tax filers capture and report certain payments. These instructions were issued to keep taxpayers in compliance with the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which passed in 2025.


To learn more,[visit the IRS website](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i1099mec) .


The IRS released an **updated fact sheet on the qualified overtime deduction** , specifying that for tax years 2026 and later, the deduction is only allowed for amounts that an employer specifically reports on an employee’s Form W-2. The new guidance, provided in[Fact Sheet 2026-13](https://www.irs.gov/pub/taxpros/fs-2026-13.pdf) , replaces a set of questions and answers issued in January 2026. The updates clarify the reporting requirements that become mandatory for tax years beginning after Dec. 31, 2025.


For more information,[visit the IRS website](https://www.irs.gov/pub/taxpros/fs-2026-13.pdf) .


The IRS provided updates on reporting[Trump Account contributions](https://www.irs.gov/trumpaccounts) in the agency’s Aug. 13 payroll industry teleconference.


Employers can report employer-funded contributions and employee salary reduction contributions to Trump Accounts under a Section 125 cafeteria plan on Form W-2, Wage and Tax Statement, in Box 12 using code TA. The form’s instructions state that code TA is used to identify employer contributions to Trump Accounts. However, because both employee salary reduction contributions under cafeteria plans and employer contributions are exempt from income tax, code TA can be used for both types. This is an exclusion from gross income, not an exemption, and is still taxable under FICA/FUTA.


Additionally, Section 128 contributions funded through salary reduction cannot be made to the employee’s own Trump Account; they must be made to the account of the employee’s dependent.


Following the Treasury’s Oct. 1 automatic enrollment, every eligible child under 18 with a valid Social Security number now has a Trump Account. A parent or guardian must claim the child’s automatically enrolled account to manage it and allow family members, friends and employers to contribute. To claim an account, a parent or guardian downloads the official Trump Accounts app, available for iOS and Android, verifies their identity and relationship to the child, reviews the child’s information and accepts the account terms. Employers can contribute up to $2,500 per year, and the total annual contribution limit from all sources cannot exceed $5,000.


For more information, visit the[TrumpAccounts.gov](https://trumpaccounts.gov/?source=govdelivery) website.


The Social Security Administration announced Oct. 14 that the **Social Security wage base** will rise to $192,300 for 2027, up from $184,500 for 2026. Social Security and Medicare tax rates will not change.


For more information,[visit the Social Security Administration website](https://www.ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbb.html) .


## State HR compliance updates


### *Arizona*


[Arizona House Bill 4168](https://www.azleg.gov/legtext/57leg/2R/laws/0140.pdf) establishes the **Unemployment Insurance Operating Fund (UIOF)** , effective Jan. 1, 2027. Managed by the Arizona Department of Economic Security (DES), the dedicated fund will cover administrative costs associated with the state’s unemployment insurance (UI) program.


The requirement applies only to experience-rated employers. It does not apply to new employers or reimbursable employers. In each quarter of calendar year 2027, an experience-rated employer must:


- pay an amount equal to 3.15% of its UI tax liability, to be deposited into the UIOF
- have its UI tax liability reduced by 3.15%


Under the law, no more than $8 million may be deposited into the UIOF in calendar year 2027, and any amount above that is deposited into the state unemployment compensation fund. The law will be repealed after Dec. 31, 2027.


Employers will report the new calculations on their UI tax and wage reports.


For federal reporting, only contributions to a state unemployment compensation fund can be reported on IRS Form 940 for the FUTA credit. Any amount contributed to the UIOF cannot be reported for FUTA credit.


For more information,[visit the Arizona Department of Economic Security website](https://des.az.gov/services/employment/unemployment-employer/unemployment-insurance-operating-fund) .


### ***California***


The California Franchise Tax Board published the[California Withholding Schedules for 2027](https://edd.ca.gov/siteassets/files/pdf_pub_ctr/27methb.pdf) , effective Jan. 1, 2027. Employers can use either **Method A (Wage Bracket Table Method)** , which is limited to wages or salaries under $1 million and has the standard deduction and exemption allowance credit built in, or **Method B (Exact Calculation Method)** , which can be used manually or by computer to calculate the exact amount to withhold.


To avoid under-withholding for married employees with employed spouses, the Franchise Tax Board recommends using the single filing status to compute withholding for the employee and spouse, or withholding an additional flat amount.


For more information,[visit the California Employment Development Department website](https://edd.ca.gov/siteassets/files/pdf_pub_ctr/27methb.pdf) .


### *Colorado*


[Colorado Senate Bill 26-121](https://leg.colorado.gov/bill_files/115752/download) sets a 56-hour weekly threshold for when agricultural employers must pay overtime to agricultural employees. Beginning Jan. 1, 2027, employers must pay an overtime rate for any time worked in excess of 56 hours in a workweek.


The overtime requirement does not apply to agricultural employees who are principally engaged in the range production of livestock on the open range, decision-making managers employed by an agricultural employer or family members of a family owner of an agricultural employer.


The law defines a “decision-making manager” as an individual primarily engaged in agricultural work who meets the minimum salary threshold, is not employed on a seasonal or temporary basis and has primary duties requiring the routine exercise of independent judgment and discretion. The individual must also either supervise two or more full-time employees or report directly to an owner or to an executive-level employee who reports to an owner.


The law also increases penalties for certain agricultural employers. An agricultural employer that willfully fails to pay wages at least three times in a five-year period may face a 10% increase in the total fine. In addition, agricultural employers with a third or subsequent willful misclassification violation within five years face a $20,000 increase in the fine and an additional $40,000 increase if the violation is not remedied within 60 days after the division’s finding.


The act applies to time worked and contracts entered into or renewed on or after its effective date.


Visit the[Colorado General Assembly website](https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/sb26-121) for more information.


### *Connecticut*


[Connecticut House Bill 5003](https://www.cga.ct.gov/2026/ACT/PA/PDF/2026PA-00012-R00HB-05003-PA.PDF) updates the state’s pay transparency requirements, effective Oct. 1, 2026.


Under the law, employers must include the wages or wage range and a general description of benefits in internal and public job advertisements. Employers may also need to provide this information to applicants before discussing or offering compensation if the position was not included in a job advertisement.


The law also requires employers to provide employees with the wage range and general description of benefits for their position upon hire, when their position changes or upon the employee’s first request.


For more information, visit the[Connecticut General Assembly](https://www.cga.ct.gov/asp/CGABillStatus/cgabillstatus.asp?selBillType=Bill&bill_num=hb5003) website.


### ***Delaware***


Delaware UI tax changes take effect Jan. 1, 2027, including an increase in the state’s taxable wage base and a new method of calculating unemployment insurance tax rates for experience-rated employers:


- **Fixed taxable wage base:** The taxable wage base rises to **$16,500** for 2027 and thereafter, completing a multiyear phase-in from **$12,500** (2025) and **$14,500** (2026). Employers pay SUI taxes only on wages up to this limit per employee each calendar year.
- **Updated experience rating structure:** The 2027 overhaul replaces the prior methodology and rate calculation approach with a structure combining a benefit ratio assessment, an employer size add-on and an industry add-on.
- **New employer rate adjustment:** Starting Jan. 1, 2027, new employers face a **1.0%** base rate plus any applicable industry rate (compared to 1.0% in 2026), until qualifying for an earned rate after at least 12 consecutive quarters of assessment reports.


For more information and a tax calculator,[visit the Delaware General Assembly website](https://legis.delaware.gov/BillDetail/141505) .


### *Kentucky*


The Kentucky Department of Revenue announced that **Kentucky’s individual standard deduction** will increase to $3,470 for 2027, up $110 from $3,360 in 2026.


The inflation-adjusted amount will be incorporated into Kentucky’s 2027 tax forms.


For more information, visit the[Kentucky Department of Revenue](https://revenue.ky.gov/News/Pages/Kentucky-DOR-Announces-2027-Standard-Deduction.aspx) website.


### *Massachusetts*


[Massachusetts Chapter 101 of the Acts of 2026](https://malegislature.gov/Laws/SessionLaws/Acts/2026/Chapter101) shifts the employer-funded portion of Paid Family and Medical Leave (PFML) contributions from medical leave to family leave beginning Jan. 1, 2027.


The law amends Section 6 of Chapter 175M of the Massachusetts General Laws, which governs PFML contributions. It swaps the percentages used in the contribution provisions for medical leave and family leave, so the portion employers fund for medical leave and the portion employers fund for family leave switch places.


The law directs the Executive Office of Labor and Workforce Development, in consultation with the Department of Family and Medical Leave, to issue guidance within 30 days of the law’s effective date on the impact for employers and employees in calendar year 2027. The guidance will include administrative adjustments intended to keep the overall balance of employee and employer contribution levels unchanged while limiting the tax burden on employees. The guidance will be available on the department’s website.


For more information,[visit the Massachusetts Legislature website](https://malegislature.gov/Laws/SessionLaws/Acts/2026/Chapter101) .


### *Missouri*


The Missouri Department of Labor and Industrial Relations’ Division of Employment Security (DES) reports that the state’s **UI taxable wage base** will decrease to $8,500 for 2027, down from $9,000 in 2026. Employers pay UI tax on each employee’s wages only up to the taxable wage base in a calendar year.


Tax rates are unchanged for 2027. The new employer rate remains 2.376% for most industries, including mining and construction, and 1.0% for nonprofit organizations described under Section 501(c)(3) of the Internal Revenue Code. These rates include applicable contribution rate adjustments. Experience rates can range from 0.0% to 6.0%, not including any maximum rate surcharge or contribution rate adjustment. DES also does not expect a federal interest assessment to be necessary for calendar year 2027.


For more information,[visit the Missouri Department of Labor and Industrial Relations website](https://labor.mo.gov/des/employers/tax-rates) .


### *Nebraska*


The Nebraska Department of Revenue issued its 2027 Circular EN. It contains updated state income tax withholding tables that employers should use for wages, pensions and annuities, and gambling winnings paid on or after Jan. 1, 2027.


For more information, visit the[Nebraska Department of Revenue](https://revenue.nebraska.gov/businesses/circular-en-nebraska-income-tax-withholding-wages-pensions-and-annuities-and-gambling) website.


[Nebraska Legislative Bill 258](https://nebraskalegislature.gov/FloorDocs/109/PDF/Engrossed/LB258.pdf) changes the state’s minimum wage and training wage provisions and creates a new youth minimum wage.


The minimum wage is $15 per hour through Dec. 31, 2026. Beginning Jan. 1, 2027, and each Jan. 1 after, the rate will increase by 1.75%. The Nebraska Department of Labor must calculate and publish the next year’s rate by Oct. 15 each year, starting Oct. 15, 2026. Student-learners in a bona fide vocational training program must be paid at least 75% of the applicable minimum wage.


Employers may pay a youth minimum wage of $13.50 per hour to employees who are at least 14 but younger than 16 and are not emancipated minors. Beginning Jan. 1, 2030, and every fifth year after, the youth minimum wage will increase by 1.5%, rounded to the nearest cent.


The training wage for new employees who are at least 16 but younger than 20 is $13.50 per hour through Dec. 31, 2026. Beginning Jan. 1, 2027, it will increase by 1.5% each year, rounded to the nearest cent. Employers may not use the training wage to replace or reduce the hours of existing employees.


Visit the[Nebraska Legislature website](https://nebraskalegislature.gov/bills/view_bill.php?DocumentID=59447) for more information.


### *New York*


New York enacted two worker-protection laws that create new requirements for construction scheduling and employee access to personnel records.


Effective Dec. 8, 2026, the[Construction Reporting Pay Act](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/bills/2025/S9843) requires a construction employee who reports for work at the employer’s request or permission to receive at least four hours of pay, or pay for the regularly scheduled shift if it is shorter. Employers also must provide two hours of pay when a scheduled construction shift is canceled with less than 12 hours’ notice. Special prevailing-wage requirements apply to covered public works projects.


Violators are subject to action by the New York State attorney general’s office and could face fines between $500 and $2,500.


Visit the[New York State Senate](https://www.nysenate.gov/) website for more information.


[New York Senate Bill 3460](https://legislation.nysenate.gov/pdf/bills/2025/S3460) , which went into effect Nov. 8, 2026, gives current and former employees the right to obtain copies of personnel records used or potentially used to make decisions about employment, promotion, transfer, additional compensation or disciplinary action. Covered records include employment applications, job and compensation information, performance evaluations, written warnings, waivers, termination notices and other disciplinary documents.


Employers generally must provide a complete copy at no cost within five business days of a written request and notify an employee within 10 days after adding information that may negatively affect the employee. Employers may limit routine reviews to twice per calendar year, but a review prompted by newly added negative information does not count toward that limit.


Employees may request that disputed information be corrected or removed. If the parties do not agree, the employee may add a written statement explaining their position, which must accompany the disputed information when it is shared with a third party. Employers also must retain complete personnel records for three years after employment ends and may not retaliate against employees for exercising their rights under the law.


Visit the[New York State Senate](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/bills/2025/S3460) website for more information.


[New York Assembly Bill 9466](https://legislation.nysenate.gov/pdf/bills/2025/A9466) extends paid family leave benefits to certain construction workers. The law defines a “construction employee” as an employee who performs construction, demolition, reconstruction, excavation, rehabilitation, repairs, renovations, alterations or improvements for multiple employers under a collective bargaining agreement.


Under the law, construction employees are eligible for family leave benefits with the covered employer they worked for immediately before the leave if they worked that employer’s normal workweek for at least 26 of the last 39 weeks. This eligibility also applies to construction employees who return to work after an unpaid leave of absence or layoff while receiving unemployment benefits. Employees remain eligible for family leave benefits only while employed with a covered employer.


The law also requires construction employees’ existing union health plan or fund benefits to remain in force for the duration of family leave. Parties to a collective bargaining agreement may agree to additional terms, such as payment of health contributions during leave.


The law takes effect on the same date as the 2025 paid family leave legislation it amends ([S. 50](https://legislation.nysenate.gov/pdf/bills/2025/S50) /[A. 4727](https://legislation.nysenate.gov/pdf/bills/2025/A4727) ), which the law sets as Jan. 1, 2027.


Visit the[New York State Senate website](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/bills/2025/A9466) for more information.


### ***Oregon***


[Oregon Senate Bill 1518](https://olis.oregonlegislature.gov/liz/2026R1/Downloads/MeasureDocument/sb1518/Enrolled) amends the state’s worker protection laws regarding home care and companionship services. The law updates two sections of Oregon law:[ORS 653.020](https://www.oregonlegislature.gov/bills_laws/ors/ors653.html) , which lists employees who are exempt from Oregon’s minimum wage and overtime requirements, and[ORS 653.547](https://www.oregonlegislature.gov/bills_laws/ors/ors653.html) , which covers domestic workers.


Under the law, the exemption for individuals employed in domestic service in a family home to provide companionship services to people who cannot care for themselves because of age or infirmity now uses the definition of companionship services in[29 C.F.R. 552.6](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-V/subchapter-A/part-552/subpart-A/section-552.6) , in effect Jan. 1, 2016. The exemption does not apply to individuals employed, singly or jointly, by a third party engaged in the business of providing home care or companionship services.


The law makes the same change to the definition of “domestic worker.” Individuals performing companionship services are excluded from the definition only if they meet the federal definition and are not employed by a third-party home care or companionship services business.


Visit the[Oregon State Legislature website](https://olis.oregonlegislature.gov/liz/2026R1/Measures/Overview/sb1518) for more information.


### *South Carolina*


The South Carolina Department of Revenue (DOR) published its **2026 Tax Legislative Update** ([Information Letter #26-23](https://dor.sc.gov/administrative-legislative-regulations-tax-legislation-update-2026) , dated Oct. 1, 2026), which summarizes significant tax and regulatory changes enacted during the 2026 legislative session. The update is organized into four categories: income taxes, bank taxes, withholding and corporate license fees; property taxes and fees in lieu of property taxes; sales and use taxes; and miscellaneous administrative and tax legislation. It also lists new and reenacted temporary provisos, which are enacted in the state budget and expire June 30, 2027, unless reenacted.


Among the income tax changes,[House Bill 4216 (Act 110)](https://www.scstatehouse.gov/sess126_2025-2026/bills/4216) reduces the state’s individual income tax brackets from three to two for tax years beginning after 2025. Taxable income of $0 to $29,999 is taxed at 1.99%, and income of $30,000 or more is taxed at 5.21% minus $966. Beginning with the 2027 tax year, the top rate of 5.21% may be reduced if state revenue projections meet certain thresholds. The DOR will also consult with the Revenue and Fiscal Affairs Office to adjust the state’s withholding tables to reflect the new tax tables and rates.


For more information,[visit the South Carolina Department of Revenue website](https://dor.sc.gov/administrative-legislative-regulations-tax-legislation-update-2026) .


### ***Virginia***


[Virginia House Bill 20](https://lis.blob.core.windows.net/files/1217658.PDF) and[Senate Bill 121](https://lis.blob.core.windows.net/files/1217662.PDF) remove the minimum wage exemption for farm laborers and farm employees. The identical laws amend[Va. Code § 40.1-28.9](https://law.lis.virginia.gov/vacode/title40.1/chapter3/section40.1-28.9/) , which defines which workers are covered by the state’s minimum wage law.


Previously, the definition of “employee” excluded any person employed as a farm laborer or farm employee. Under the laws, farm laborers and farm employees are no longer excluded from the definition. Other exclusions, such as those for caddies, certain students, babysitters who work fewer than 10 hours per week and temporary foreign workers, remain in place.


The laws take effect Jan. 1, 2027.


Visit the[Virginia General Assembly website](https://lis.virginia.gov/) for more information.


### ***Washington***


[Washington Substitute Senate Bill 6014](https://lawfilesext.leg.wa.gov/biennium/2025-26/Pdf/Bills/Session%20Laws/Senate/6014-S.SL.pdf?q=20261110090603) refines the state’s pregnancy-related accommodation requirements by clarifying when employers may require written certification and by protecting employees’ personal information. The law takes effect Jan. 1, 2027.


Under the law, an employer may request written certification from an employee’s treating healthcare professional regarding the need for a reasonable accommodation. Employers may not request certification for certain accommodations listed in[RCW 49.92.010(6)(a), (b), (d) and (h)](https://app.leg.wa.gov/RCW/default.aspx?cite=49.92.010) , or for limits on lifting over 17 pounds.


The law also makes records filed with or maintained by the Washington Department of Labor and Industries confidential if they reveal the identity of or contain personal information about an employee or applicant who filed a complaint, requested assistance or participated in an investigation. Personal information includes the individual’s name, address, telephone number, electronic contact information, identifying photograph and any medical or health information related to pregnancy or childbirth.


The department may release statistical or summary data that do not identify an individual. Information may also be disclosed to the complainant’s employer when necessary for a fair determination of the issues in an investigation, to public employees performing their official duties, in court or administrative proceedings when required by law or necessary to fairly determine the issues, and to the complainant.


Visit the[Washington State Legislature website](https://app.leg.wa.gov/billsummary?Year=2025&BillNumber=6014) for more information.


### ***Wisconsin***


The Wisconsin Department of Revenue (DOR) issued its[Withholding Tax Update 2026-1](https://www.revenue.wi.gov/withholdingtaxupdate/26-1.pdf) in October 2026, which outlines withholding and reporting requirements for employers and payers. Key points include:


- **W-2 differences:** Because Wisconsin’s Internal Revenue Code differs from the federal code, 2026 Form W-2 Wisconsin wages (Box 16) may not match federal wages for employees receiving compensation under certain exclusions, including combat zone pay, student loan payments under education assistance programs, employer contributions to Trump Accounts, dependent care assistance above the Wisconsin exemption amount and certain fringe benefits.
- **Agricultural labor:** Wisconsin income tax withholding is not required on payments for agricultural labor, such as H-2A workers, though employers may withhold voluntarily if both parties agree.
- **Retirement and pension payments:** Withholding is not required, but recipients may request it in writing, and the amount withheld from each payment must be at least $5.
- **Filing deadlines:** For tax year 2026, wage statements, information returns and the annual reconciliation (Form WT-7) are due Feb. 1, 2027. Employers filing 10 or more wage statements or information returns must file electronically, and Forms WT-6 and WT-7 must be filed electronically unless a waiver is approved.
- **Form 1099-R:** Form 1099-Rs with Wisconsin withholding must be filed directly with the DOR. The combined federal/state filing program is not an approved option for these forms.
- **Form 1099 thresholds:** Wisconsin has not adopted the federal increase of the Form 1099-MISC, 1099-NEC and 1099-R reporting threshold from $600 to $2,000, so payers may need to file with Wisconsin even if they are not required to file with the IRS.
- **Filing systems:** The IRS FIRE system is no longer available as of Jan. 1, 2027, and the IRS Publication 1220 format will sunset in September 2027. The DOR will accept FIRE files for 2026 and earlier tax years and encourages filers to adopt IRIS-formatted files, My Tax Account or approved payroll software.
- **Penalties:** A $10 penalty applies for each late, incorrect or incomplete wage statement or information return, and for each paper return filed when electronic filing is required.
- **Transportation fringe benefits:** The 2026 exclusion limit is $340 per month for qualified parking and for commuter highway vehicle transportation and transit passes. The 2027 amounts are not yet available.


For more information,[visit the Wisconsin Department of Revenue website](https://www.revenue.wi.gov/withholdingtaxupdate/26-1.pdf) .
